---
title: "Origins (1961–1977)"
---

## The Political Behavior Archive, 1961

UCLA's data archive lineage begins with Dwaine Marvick, a UCLA political
science professor who founded the **Political Behavior Archive (PBA)** in
1961. Rice & Southall (2016), *The Data Librarian's Handbook*, Table 1.1,
situates it in the field's founding cohort: "UCLA Data Services, 1961" ranks
as the fourth-oldest social-science data library or service in their sample,
after Roper Center (1957), Berkeley (1958), and GESIS (1960), and ahead of
ICPSR itself (1962).

## Why archives like this one emerged

UCLA's archive is one local expression of a broader postwar development in
empirical social science. It wasn't the product of a single, unified
"movement" with one agreed rationale. It's better described as a **family of
related infrastructure-building projects**, and contemporaries were already
discussing them comparatively by the mid-1960s: Ralph Bisco's 1966 review in
the *American Political Science Review* treats Roper, Berkeley, Michigan, and
European archives as one emerging domain.

The multi-causal explanation that survives scrutiny: the growth of survey
research and behavioral political science produced large bodies of reusable
observations. The expense of new surveys created an incentive to preserve and
share existing ones. Punch cards, tabulating equipment, and later magnetic
tape made large-scale reuse technically possible. Foundations, federal
agencies, and membership consortia made the resulting infrastructure
sustainable. Training new quantitative researchers wasn't incidental either.
At ICPSR especially, it was a founding purpose, not a service layered on
afterward.

One correction to how this was framed internally: **centralized campus
computing is better documented as an enabling condition and a bottleneck than
as the originating cause.** The clearest founding documents (ICPSR's 1962
memorandum, Roper's founding rationale, the UK Data Archive's founding
committee) foreground research demand, cost, and coordination problems.
Computing shows up as the means the solution operated through, not the reason
the problem became urgent.

That framing holds up against the actual founding document. Warren Miller's
August 1962 memo to ISR director Rensis Likert, laying out the case for what
became ICPSR, opens with the research problem, not a technology problem: "The
rapid increase in scholarly interest in the kinds of data which survey
research can provide has far outstripped the availability of the survey
mechanism to the interested scholar. This hiatus has become a matter of
serious concern to many social scientists." Computing gets no mention in his
stated rationale at all.

## A founding member of ICPSR, 1962

UCLA was among the founding member institutions of the **Inter-university
Consortium for Political and Social Research (ICPSR)**, established in 1962
by political scientist Warren E. Miller to solve an organizational bottleneck
in the production of empirical political science. Heavily demanded
election-study data needed permanent preservation and dissemination, but so
did training new researchers to use it and coordinating a scattered research
community. Its founding memorandum set four objectives, conceived together
rather than as separable services: developing data resources, formal
quantitative training, stimulating new research, and a clearinghouse on
ongoing work.

UCLA's current Dataverse collection page credits this "through [Marvick's]
efforts" and states UCLA was one of **8** founding members. The full
institutional membership at founding was larger than 8: Erik Austin, a
longtime ICPSR staff member, compiled a list of 22 original institutions from
membership records, Michigan plus 21 others. Miller's own August 1962 memo
goes further: it names the members directly, dated "as of July 30, 1962," and
lists 21, "University of California at Los Angeles" among them. Either way,
UCLA's founding-member status is confirmed against the actual 1962 document,
not just a later recollection.

That looked like the end of the "8" question, and then it got more
interesting. ICPSR's current director, Maggie Levenstein, used the same "8"
figure independently during a UCLA visit, not obviously copying UCLA's own
page. And ICPSR's own institutional archive at the Bentley Historical
Library, per its finding aid, holds a folder titled "Committee of Eight,
Correspondence and Minutes, 1962-1963." That's a plausible, specific referent
for "8" that has nothing to do with the 21/22-institution membership count:
a smaller founding committee, not the full roster of dues-paying members. If
that's right, both numbers could be correct, describing two different things.
Not confirmed. Nobody has read that folder yet.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The headcount is fixed. The personal-role claim is now plausible, still not proven.
UCLA's founding-member status is confirmed against the primary 1962 document
itself. The personal-role question moved, but didn't resolve. No source found
so far, including Miller's own founding memo, gives documentary evidence
Marvick had a formal role in founding ICPSR in 1962. ICPSR's first annual
report names its initial council members, and he isn't on it. But a 1999
memorial by Heinz Eulau, a colleague of both men, establishes something new:
Marvick and Warren Miller were personal friends and research collaborators a
full decade before either the archive or ICPSR existed, together at
Michigan's Survey Research Center in the early 1950s. That's a real,
documented channel through which "through his efforts" could plausibly be
true, even though nobody has yet found a document that says so directly. His
formally documented ICPSR role remains governing-board service starting
**1964**, rising to **chair of the ICPR Council in 1966-67** (per Eulau,
more precise than earlier sources), all after founding, not during it.
"Marvick helped connect UCLA to the emerging ICPSR network, likely through
his friendship with Miller" is now a defensible sentence. "Through his
efforts, UCLA was one of the founding members" still isn't, on direct
documentary evidence. See [Sources & Open Questions](sources.qmd) for the
full research trail.
:::

### Marvick's own scholarly profile

Apart from the ICPSR question, Marvick's documented research program explains
why an archive like this would plausibly come from him specifically: survey
methods brought from Michigan in 1954, statistical approaches to political
behavior, and, per a UC memorial, work as "an early advocate and practitioner
of computer applications to political data." His papers include election
surveys, computer codebooks, and printouts spanning Los Angeles politics, the
Detroit Area Study, West German elections, and Indian electorate surveys.

Eulau's 1999 memorial fills in the earlier chapter of that career. Marvick
arrived at Michigan's Survey Research Center in the early 1950s, fresh off a
Columbia PhD, as a Carnegie Fellow, working alongside Morris Janowitz on a
restudy of the Center's 1952 election data. Warren Miller was there too,
still finishing his own PhD. The two became close, personally and
professionally, years before either left Michigan, Miller for a stint at
Berkeley, Marvick for UCLA, where Eulau writes he "took deep Western roots."
By 1956 Marvick was already organizing national conversations in the field:
he named the three panels for the first APSA meeting sessions devoted
exclusively to political behavior. He chaired APSA's own 1972 annual meeting
program at Eulau's request, and in 1988 spent two days interviewing Eulau for
the APSA oral history project, eight double-sided tapes, at his home in Los
Angeles.

::: {.callout-note}
## What's still not documented: why 1961, specifically
No source found so far, including Eulau's detailed personal memoir, states
Marvick's own reason for founding the archive in 1961. That absence is
notable on its own: Eulau's memoir covers Marvick's career in real depth,
APSA leadership roles, ICPR council chairmanship, his broad intellectual
range, his family, and never once mentions the archive. The scholarly profile
above makes founding an archive a plausible, well-contextualized move for
him, but his personal motivation remains an inference, not a documented fact.
His own papers (correspondence, project records from roughly 1959 to 1964)
are still the likeliest place that would actually resolve this. Marvick died
of a stroke in late February 1999, four weeks after Miller; any direct
account would have to come from those papers or from people who knew him,
not from him.
:::

## Merger into the Survey Research Center, 1964 (disputed)

Three internal sources (two 2017 slide decks and the Dataverse About page)
agree that the archive merged into UCLA's **Survey Research Center (SRC)** in
1964, "under Eve Fielder." One deck adds detail: the PBA "merged with a
planned Archive Data Library the SRC was to house."

::: {.callout-warning}
## Open conflict: was Fielder SRC's director from 1964?
A published obituary for Eve Fielder states she became SRC's **first director
in 1976**, the same year external evidence (UCLA's General Catalog) places
SRC's incorporation into ISSR. This directly conflicts with the "1964, under
Fielder" framing repeated across three internal sources. Two readings are
possible: SRC existed from 1964 under a different, unidentified founding
director and Fielder took over later, or the "1964 + Fielder" framing in the
internal decks compresses two separate events into one. **Not resolved.** See
[Sources & Open Questions](sources.qmd#pre-1977-connective-tissue).
:::

## Toward 1977

What's well-established: by the mid-1970s the archive was operating inside
SRC, and by 1976–77 it was reconstituted as a service unit of the Institute
for Social Science Research (ISSR). Exactly how SRC's 1976 incorporation into
ISSR relates to the archive's own December 1977 establishment as a named ISSR
unit is covered in the next chapter, [The ISSR Era](issr-era.qmd).
